Reviews + new category, published Oct 19, 2026. Angle: failure story. I slid a two-foot cheater pipe over the OPEN end of a 13mm and leaned on a rusted caliper bracket bolt; the jaws spread like a duck bill, the bolt rounded, and the job finished with an extractor set. Title: 'Best Wrench Set: I Bent One in Half' (35 chars). Core message: a combination wrench is two tools in one, and the wrong end on a stuck bolt is what rounds it. Value block: open end vs box end (2 corner contacts vs a closed ring that surrounds the nut; open end only engages in 15-degree steps); the rule (box end to break, open end to spin) plus the one job only the open end can do (fittings and flare nuts, because a closed ring cannot slide over a line, which is why flare nut wrenches exist); 6-point vs 12-point box ends (6 contacts the flats and survives rust, 12 doubles the access angles; same rule as the impact-socket post, cross-linked); length/offset/stubby (15-degree offset for knuckle clearance, long pattern for turning force, stubby for alternator/starter/intake bolts with no swing room). Hidden door: the adjustable (crescent) wrench rounds more nuts than any other tool, two contacts plus a worm gear that backs off under load. Middle twist (contradiction): the ratcheting head is the WEAKEST end and the most expensive one, a small pawl in a ring of teeth built to spin a bolt already broken loose; strip the pawl with a cheater pipe or an impact shock and it freewheels, while the fixed box end has no pawl and takes a load the ratcheting one cannot. notes: Reviews + new category 'tire-inflator' (Tire Inflators, short: Inflators), published Oct 21, 2026. Angle: the 150 PSI on the box is a CEILING, not a SPEED, and the number that decides your wait is flow (CFM / L per min). Opening failure story: a $25 12V pump filled two tires on a cold November morning and then hit its thermal cutout on the third, leaving a tire at 28 psi while I waited. Value block (5 H2s): (1) pressure ceiling vs flow, VIAIR 1.97 CFM @ 0 psi means less at 32 psi, NOCO publishes 36 LPM, the cheap pump prints no flow at all; wrapper rule 'Buy flow, not pressure'; (2) duty cycle is the real limit, VIAIR 25 min @ 30 psi, cheap pumps ~10 on / 10 off, buried in the manual; (3) your 12V socket is usually a 15 amp / ~180 W circuit, which is why VIAIR's 20 A max draw ships with battery clamps and NOCO's 10 A/138 W uses the socket, and why the DEWALT's three power sources matter; (4) the number you fill to is the door jamb sticker, not the sidewall max, with 1 psi per 10 F, 1-2 psi/month permeation, TPMS at ~25% below placard, and hot tires reading 3-5 psi high. Middle twist (verified contradiction): the $31.99 AstroAI advertises 150 PSI / 35 L per min while the $99.95 NOCO AIR10 advertises 60 PSI / 36 L per min. Nearly identical flow, opposite pressure claims, and the lower-ceiling pump costs 3x. Pressure is a marketing ladder; what you pay for is duty cycle, gauge accuracy (NOCO dwell), and warranty. Ritual 'The Test': 25->35 psi on one tire, then three more with no cooldown, then each built-in gauge checked against a separate digital gauge. Result: preset pumps shut off where set, non-preset pumps read a few pounds high while hot (hot air in a hot hose), 25 min duty cycle pumps finished four tires, small ones paused. Reviews + new category 'brake-bleeder' (Brake Bleeders, short: Bleeders), published Oct 23, 2026. Angle: the bubbles in the bleeder hose are the tool lying to you, not your brakes. Opening failure story: a $22 vacuum pump on a 2003 Corolla right rear caliper, half a quart of fluid through one corner, hose full of bubbles that would not stop, still-soft pedal. Core message + wrapper rule: 'Chase fluid, not bubbles.' Value block (4 H2s): (1) the bleeder screw seals at its TIP, crack it a quarter turn and the threads become a second path, so the pump pulls room air in and the bubble stream never ends; the fix is 2 or 3 wraps of PTFE tape on the threads (not the tip) or a dab of grease; micro bubbles mean nothing, a gap in the fluid column is what matters. (2) the three families and where each one puts the pressure: check valve + pedal (needs a helper or a pedal prop), vacuum at the caliper (pedal never moves), pressure at the reservoir (10-15 psi, shop method, fails when the cap does not seal). (3) bleeding order farthest from the master cylinder first (RR, LR, RF, LF), quarter turn on the screw, hose end kept under the fluid surface, close the screw before the pedal comes up, box end or 6-point on the bleeder screw (8-10mm Japanese, 3/8 domestic), one quart of fluid per flush plus one if you swap a caliper, old fluid to a parts store for recycling, 2-3 year flush interval because brake fluid is hygroscopic. (4) HIDDEN DOOR: do not push the pedal to the floor. A master cylinder bore pits past its normal travel; the cup seals slide into that rough section and tear, which is no pedal plus a new master cylinder. Fix is a block of wood under the pedal, or a vacuum/pressure bleeder where the pedal never moves. Middle twist (contradiction): a borrowed $72 Motive pressure bleeder lost to a $22.89 check valve bottle, not because the bottle is better but because the pressure bleeder is a tank, a pump, and a CAP, and the cap is the whole product; a universal chain cap sprayed fluid at 15 psi on the third corner. So reviews on pressure bleeders were written by people whose cap happened to fit. Ritual 'The Test': same rear caliper, three methods, 100 ml marks on the catch container, phone timer, pedal checked after each. Check valve bottle + pedal prop: clean solid column at about 200 ml, hard pedal, roughly 12 minutes including jacking. Hand vacuum pump: same 200 ml in under two minutes, but five minutes of thread-leak bubbles until the PTFE tape went on. Pressure bleeder: fastest and cleanest until the universal cap let go and sprayed the intake manifold.
